Personal Loan Campaign Full Code Solution - Maneesh Anand K N¶

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

AllLife Bank is a US bank that has a growing customer base. The majority of these customers are liability customers (depositors) with varying sizes of deposits. The number of customers who are also borrowers (asset customers) is quite small, and the bank is interested in expanding this base rapidly to bring in more loan business and in the process, earn more through the interest on loans. In particular, the management wants to explore ways of converting its liability customers to personal loan customers (while retaining them as depositors).

A campaign that the bank ran last year for liability customers showed a healthy conversion rate of over 9% success. This has encouraged the retail marketing department to devise campaigns with better target marketing to increase the success ratio.

You as a Data scientist at AllLife bank have to build a model that will help the marketing department to identify the potential customers who have a higher probability of purchasing the loan.

Objective¶

To predict whether a liability customer will buy personal loans, to understand which customer attributes are most significant in driving purchases, and identify which segment of customers to target more.

Data Dictionary¶

  • ID: Customer ID
  • Age: Customer’s age in completed years
  • Experience: #years of professional experience
  • Income: Annual income of the customer (in thousand dollars)
  • ZIP Code: Home Address ZIP code.
  • Family: the Family size of the customer
  • CCAvg: Average spending on credit cards per month (in thousand dollars)
  • Education: Education Level. 1: Undergrad; 2: Graduate;3: Advanced/Professional
  • Mortgage: Value of house mortgage if any. (in thousand dollars)
  • Personal_Loan: Did this customer accept the personal loan offered in the last campaign? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Securities_Account: Does the customer have securities account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CD_Account: Does the customer have a certificate of deposit (CD) account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Online: Do customers use internet banking facilities? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CreditCard: Does the customer use a credit card issued by any other Bank (excluding All life Bank)? (0: No, 1: Yes)

Observations on the attributes¶

  • Age:

    • The age distribution ranges from 23 to 67 years with a mean of 45.34 years.
    • The median (50th percentile) is 45, which aligns with the mean, indicating a symmetric distribution.
    • The standard deviation is 11.46, suggesting a moderately spread-out distribution.

  • Experience:

    • The range is from -3 to 43 years.
    • Negative numbers need to be treated in the dataset
    • The mean (20.1) and median (20) are close, indicating a symmetric distribution.
    • The standard deviation (11.47) is similar to age (experience and age typically correlate).

  • Income:

    • Income ranges from $8k to $224k with a mean of $73.77k.
    • The median (50th percentile) is $64k, which is lower than the mean ($73.77k), indicating a right-skewed distribution (due to presence of high earners).
    • The IQR indicates most incomes fall between $39k and $98k.

  • Family:

    • Household sizes range from 1 to 4, with a mean of 2.40.
    • The median is 2, indicating most people have small to medium-sized families.
    • This column is most likely categorical despite being represented numerically.

  • CCAvg:

    • The range is from $0 to $10k, with a mean of $1.94k.
    • The median is $1.5k, slightly lower than the mean, again indicating a slight right-skewed distribution.
    • The 75th percentile is $2.5k, meaning most people spend below this amount.

  • Education:

    • The mean is 1.88, suggesting a fairly balanced distribution of education levels.

  • Mortgage:

    • The values range from $0 to $635k, but the median is $0, meaning most people do not have a mortgage.
    • The 75th percentile is $101k, showing that a minority of people have high mortgage values.
    • The high standard deviation ($101.7k) suggests a highly skewed distribution.

  • Personal_Loan:

    • Most do not have personal loans - Only 9.6% (mean = 0.096) of people have a personal loan, as the median is 0

  • Securities_Account:

    • Similar to personal loans, most customers do not have a securities account - Only 10.4% of people have one (mean = 0.104).

  • CD_Account:

    • Only 6% of people have a CD account, suggesting it is rarer than securities accounts & personal loans.

  • Online:

    • 59.7% of customers use online banking (mean = 0.597).
    • The median is 1, meaning more than half of the customers use online banking

  • CreditCard

    • 29.4% of customers own a credit card issued by the bank.
    • The median is 0 - most customers do not own a credit card issued by the bank.

#Function to plot both histogram and boxplot

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram

    # Calculate and plot mean and median only if the feature is numeric
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[feature]):
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
      )  # Add mean to the histogram
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].median(), color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )  # Add median to the histogram
    else:
      #add mode
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mode()[0], color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )
In [355]:
# function to create labeled barplots

def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

# Function for stacked barplot

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):

    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

### function to plot distributions wrt target

def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Questions:¶

  1. What is the distribution of mortgage attribute? Are there any noticeable patterns or outliers in the distribution?
  2. How many customers have credit cards?
  3. What are the attributes that have a strong correlation with the target attribute (personal loan)?
  4. How does a customer's interest in purchasing a loan vary with their age?
  5. How does a customer's interest in purchasing a loan vary with their education?

Answers¶

  1. Mortgage demonstrates an extreme right skewed distribution with many outliers. Majority of the customers do not have mortgages and many have mortgages ranging from $80k to $250k.
  2. 29.4% (~1.5k) customers have credit cards
  3. Not many attributes have strong correlation with "Personal Loan" attribute. Income has a weak correlation of 0.5
  4. Customers between the ages of 35 to 55 availed bank's personal loan facility
  5. It is seen from the data that customers with higher education (75%) availed personal loan facility (and hence an increased interest)

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Our model aims to predict which customers are likely to be interested in a personal loan. It is crucial to understand the two types of errors the model can make:

  1. False Positive (FP): Incorrectly Predicting Interest
  • Prediction: The model predicts that the customer is interested in a personal loan.
  • Reality: The customer is not interested.
  • Impact: The model wastes probable crucial resources (marketing spend, staff time) on a non-prospective customer.
  1. False Negative (FN): Missing Interested Customers
  • Prediction: The model predicts that the customer is not interested in a personal loan.
  • Reality: The customer is interested.
  • Impact: The bank misses a potential loan opportunity and loses potential revenue.

Prioritizing Errors: FN vs. FP

The relative importance of False Positives and False Negatives depends on the bank's objectives:

  • False Negatives (FN) are often more costly. Missing a genuinely interested customer translates directly to lost revenue and lower loan disbursement rates.
  • False Positives (FP) can also be detrimental. While not as immediately impactful as missing a sale, high FP rates lead to wasted marketing spend and potentially damage customer relationships (e.g., irritating customers with irrelevant offers).

** Minimizing Losses: Reducing False Negatives **

To reduce the costly impact of False Negatives (missing interested customers), we need to prioritize strategies that improve our ability to identify these individuals.

  1. Optimize for Higher Recall (While Maintaining Acceptable Precision): Recall measures the model's ability to find all positive cases (interested customers). We should aim for a higher recall, meaning fewer interested customers are missed. However, we must monitor precision (the accuracy of positive predictions) to avoid a scenario where the model flags everyone as interested just to increase recall.

  2. Utilize the F1-Score (Balance Precision and Recall): The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It provides a single metric to evaluate the overall performance of the model, balancing the trade-off between False Positives and False Negatives. Maximizing the F1-score will improve the model's ability to accurately identify both interested and uninterested customers.

In summary, we need to carefully tune our model to achieve a good balance between capturing interested customers (high recall) and avoiding unnecessary outreach to uninterested customers (reasonable precision). The F1-score serves as a valuable metric for guiding this optimization process.

Model Performance Improvement¶

Logistic Regression¶

In [392]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))

# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Decision Tree (default)¶

First, let's create functions to calculate different metrics and confusion matrix so that we don't have to use the same code repeatedly for each model.

  • The model_performance_classification_sklearn function will be used to check the model performance of models.
  • The confusion_matrix_sklearn function will be used to plot confusion matrix.
In [397]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [398]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

Decision Tree (Pre-pruning)¶

  • Hyperparameter tuning is crucial because it directly affects the performance of a model.
  • Unlike model parameters which are learned during training, hyperparameters need to be set before training.
  • Effective hyperparameter tuning helps in improving the performance and robustness of the model.
  • The below custom loop for hyperparameter tuning iterates over predefined parameter values to identify the best model based on the metric of choice (recall score).
In [409]:
# Define the parameters of the tree to iterate over
#max_depth_values = np.arange(2,16,2)
#max_leaf_nodes_values=np.arange(2,14,2)
#min_samples_split_values=np.arange(2,10,2)

max_depth_values = np.arange(2, 16, 2)
max_leaf_nodes_values = np.arange(2, 200, 25)
min_samples_split_values = np.arange(2, 100, 10)

# Initialize variables to store the best model and its performance
best_estimator = None
best_score_diff = float('inf')
best_test_score = 0.0

# Iterate over all combinations of the specified parameter values
for max_depth in max_depth_values:
    for max_leaf_nodes in max_leaf_nodes_values:
        for min_samples_split in min_samples_split_values:

            # Initialize the tree with the current set of parameters
            estimator = DecisionTreeClassifier(
                max_depth=max_depth,
                max_leaf_nodes=max_leaf_nodes,
                min_samples_split=min_samples_split,
                class_weight='balanced',
                random_state=RANDOM_STATE_SEED
            )

            # Fit the model to the training data
            estimator.fit(X_train, y_train)

            # Make predictions on the training and test sets
            y_train_pred = estimator.predict(X_train)
            y_test_pred = estimator.predict(X_test)

            # Calculate recall scores for training and test sets
            train_recall_score = recall_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
            test_recall_score = recall_score(y_test, y_test_pred)

            # Calculate the absolute difference between training and test recall scores
            score_diff = abs(train_recall_score - test_recall_score)

            # Update the best estimator and best score if the current one has a smaller score difference
            if (score_diff < best_score_diff) & (test_recall_score > best_test_score):
                best_score_diff = score_diff
                best_test_score = test_recall_score
                best_estimator = estimator

# creating an instance of the best model
model1 = best_estimator

# Print the best parameters
print("Best parameters found:")
print(f"Max depth: {best_estimator.max_depth}")
print(f"Max leaf nodes: {best_estimator.max_leaf_nodes}")
print(f"Min samples split: {best_estimator.min_samples_split}")
print(f"Best test recall score: {best_test_score}")

Best parameters found:
Max depth: 2
Max leaf nodes: 27
Min samples split: 2
Best test recall score: 1.0

Decision Tree (Post Pruning)¶

In [418]:
# Create an instance of the decision tree model
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)

# Compute the cost complexity pruning path for the model using the training data
path = clf.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)

# Extract the array of effective alphas from the pruning path
ccp_alphas = abs(path.ccp_alphas)

# Extract the array of total impurities at each alpha along the pruning path
impurities = path.impurities

# Create a figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Plot the total impurities versus effective alphas, excluding the last value,
# using markers at each data point and connecting them with steps
ax.plot(ccp_alphas[:-1], impurities[:-1], marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")

# Set the x-axis label
ax.set_xlabel("Effective Alpha")

# Set the y-axis label
ax.set_ylabel("Total impurity of leaves")

# Set the title of the plot
ax.set_title("Total Impurity vs Effective Alpha for training set");
plt.show()
  • Next, we train a decision tree using the effective alphas.
  • The last value in ccp_alphas is the alpha value that prunes the whole tree, leaving the corresponding tree with one node.
In [421]:
# Initialize an empty list to store the decision tree classifiers
clfs = []

# Iterate over each ccp_alpha value extracted from cost complexity pruning path
for ccp_alpha in ccp_alphas:
    # Create an instance of the DecisionTreeClassifier
    clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=ccp_alpha, random_state=42)

    # Fit the classifier to the training data
    clf.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Append the trained classifier to the list
    clfs.append(clf)

# Print the number of nodes in the last tree along with its ccp_alpha value
print(
    "Number of nodes in the last tree is {} with ccp_alpha {}".format(
        clfs[-1].tree_.node_count, ccp_alphas[-1]
    )
)

Number of nodes in the last tree is 1 with ccp_alpha 0.05206542558865251
  • Moving ahead, we remove the last element in clfs and ccp_alphas as it corresponds to a trivial tree with only one node.
In [422]:
clfs = clfs[:-1]
ccp_alphas = ccp_alphas[:-1]

# Extract the number of nodes in each tree classifier
node_counts = [clf.tree_.node_count for clf in clfs]

# Extract the maximum depth of each tree classifier
depth = [clf.tree_.max_depth for clf in clfs]

# Create a figure and a set of subplots
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

# Plot the number of nodes versus ccp_alphas on the first subplot
ax[0].plot(ccp_alphas, node_counts, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[0].set_xlabel("Alpha")
ax[0].set_ylabel("Number of nodes")
ax[0].set_title("Number of nodes vs Alpha")

# Plot the depth of tree versus ccp_alphas on the second subplot
ax[1].plot(ccp_alphas, depth, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[1].set_xlabel("Alpha")
ax[1].set_ylabel("Depth of tree")
ax[1].set_title("Depth vs Alpha")

# Adjust the layout of the subplots to avoid overlap
fig.tight_layout()

train_f1_scores = []  # Initialize an empty list to store F1 scores for training set for each decision tree classifier

# Iterate through each decision tree classifier in 'clfs'
for clf in clfs:
    # Predict labels for the training set using the current decision tree classifier
    pred_train = clf.predict(X_train)

    # Calculate the F1 score for the training set predictions compared to true labels
    f1_train = f1_score(y_train, pred_train)

    # Append the calculated F1 score to the train_f1_scores list
    train_f1_scores.append(f1_train)

test_f1_scores = []  # Initialize an empty list to store F1 scores for test set for each decision tree classifier

# Iterate through each decision tree classifier in 'clfs'
for clf in clfs:
    # Predict labels for the test set using the current decision tree classifier
    pred_test = clf.predict(X_test)

    # Calculate the F1 score for the test set predictions compared to true labels
    f1_test = f1_score(y_test, pred_test)

    # Append the calculated F1 score to the test_f1_scores list
    test_f1_scores.append(f1_test)

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

Actionable Insights:

  • The Logistic Regression model achieves high accuracy, but its moderate recall score indicates that it's missing a significant portion of potential loan acceptors. The relatively high precision suggests that when it does predict loan acceptance, it's generally correct. The goal for using logistic regression is to determine how good the model is compared to the "post-pruning decision tree model".

  • I believe that there are two aspects of loan availing that needs to be covered:

    1. Providing incentives for customers to utilize the loan facility
    2. Loan approval/acceptance vs loans applied details are not provided in the dataset (liability or asset customers)

  • This being noted, following insights hold true:

    • Decision tree with post-pruning is the best model to fit in. It gives the highest recall rate (meaning it reduced the False Negative data classification).
    • Income, Family, Education_Undergraduate and CCAvg are the most important attributes in determining if a customer will avail a personal loan from AllLife bank.
    • The top 2 attributes (Income and CCAvg) are consistently ranked as the most important across all three models. This suggests that these are indeed strong predictors of loan acceptance.
    • Of the customers who availed personal loan during the previous campaign - 50% of the customers had income in the range of $125k - $175k.
    • Remaining attributes (other than Income, Family,Education_Undergraduate) could be ignored as they do not have much gini importance/significance.

  • There is an opportunity here to evaluate the importance of "CD Account" attribute. Logistic Regression vs Decision tree analysis show a discrepancy in its importance. In the positive scenario, CD Account holders will need to be prioritized and subjected to targeted strategic planning.

  • When we analyze the three feature importance plots (default, pre-pruning and post-pruning):

    • The most striking change is the massive increase in the importance of Income in the Pre-Pruning model (0.78). It completely overshadows all other features.
    • Education_Undergraduate, Family attributes have similar importance in Default and post-pruning models (except in Pre-Pruning model)
    • CCAvg attribute has a consistent, small amount of importance in all three models.
    • This might lead us to interpret that the pre-pruning model's focus on income is high, performing well in training data and hence overfitting in the pre-pruning model.

  • When we analyze the performance of the three models on training data:

    • The default Decision Tree achieves perfect accuracy, recall, and precision on the training data, indicating that it has completely memorized the training set. This is an indication of overfitting.
    • The pre-pruning model has a poor precision score (0.312682), despite perfect value for recall. This means the model is labelling results with a lot of false positives.
    • The post-pruning model achieves high scores for accuracy (0.992286), recall (0.934985), precision (0.980519), and F1 (0.957211). This has the better performance amongst the three models considered.

  • When we analyze the performance of the three models on test data:

    • The training data performance showed that the default model was overfitting because it attained an accuracy of 1. Now, reviewing the test performance - the data is indeed overfitting.
    • Pre-pruning model performs the lowest on the testing set. While it achieves perfect recall (1.000000), the precision is a low 0.339093. This confirms our suspicion that the pre-pruning model is severely overfitting to the training data. It is predicting that almost everyone will accept a loan, which is why it gets all the actual positives correct (high recall),but also misclassifies a huge number of negatives as positives (low precision).
    • The post-pruning model achieves the highest accuracy (0.986000), the highest precision (0.947368), and a very good recall (0.917197), resulting in the highest F1-score (0.932039). This indicates that pruning has been effective in improving the model's generalization performance and in reducing the impact of CD account.
    • The default Decision Tree performs reasonably well, but is slightly outperformed by the post-pruning model. This indicates that pruning has helped to improve the model's ability to generalize to unseen data.
    • Pruning has been essential in this project and selected data split.

Business Recommendations

  1. Core Targeting Strategies (Based on Primary Model Drivers):

  • High-Income Targeting: AllLife Bank should continue to prioritize targeted campaigns for high-income customers. However, recognizing that "Income" attribute is not sufficient in isolation. Instead of broad, untailored messaging, focus on showcasing how personal loans can help this segment achieve their financial goals (e.g., investments, home improvements, luxury purchases). Channels: Direct mail, personalized emails, online ads targeting high-income demographics.

  • Tailored Family-Focused Offers: Design loan products specifically catering to the needs of larger families (3-4 members). Consider marketing messages highlighting how loans can address common family expenses like education, healthcare, or home upgrades. Channels: Targeted online advertising, partnerships with family-oriented organizations.

  • Re-evaluate Education: Acknowledge the importance of the educational aspect of the undergraduate segment, as well as if there are any trends within the professional and graduate markets.

  1. Addressing the "CD Account" Opportunity:
  • Deep Dive Investigation: Initiate a thorough investigation into the relationship between CD Account ownership and loan acceptance. Analyze whether "CD Account" is more predictive within specific income bands, age groups, or family sizes. This will either highlight a bad data situation, or potentially allow the feature to be more optimized to better represent trends.
  • Craft specific marketing campaigns highlighting the benefits of personal loans to CD account holders.
  1. Optimizing the Customer Experience:

  • Simplify Application Process: Carefully review the data collected during the application process. The bank can then consider whether this data has an appropriate balance. It is important to also ensure there are minimal operational and legal conflicts with the removal of these features.

  • High-Touch/Contact for high-potential customers: Especially with pre-existing relationships as this is an internal database. It might be a great way to give some personalized service if we can find users in CD/mortgage/securities.

  1. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Model Refinement:

  • Track Performance Meticulously: Implement rigorous tracking and monitoring of campaign performance, focusing not just on overall metrics, but also on the performance within different customer segments (example: CD account holders vs. non-holders). This applies to both Logistic Regression and Decision Tree models.

  • Challenge the Model: The current "best" model ignores CD account feature.

*Continuous Refinement: Continue to check what features are or are not important. Also, evaluate for data drift (change in input data) or decay (change in the input and output relationships).

  1. Recommendations Regarding Model Choice and Justification:

  • Post-Pruning is the Best Tool: Continue to iterate on improving existing models.

  • Clear Communication of Trade-offs: When presenting results to stakeholders, clearly communicate that the importance and inclusion of the "CD Account" is not perfect and it may give out skewed results.

Predicting on test data points (Extra)¶

%%time

# making a prediction
y_pred = model2.predict(X_test)

# Create a DataFrame with actual values, predictions, and input features
predictions_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Actual': y_test,
    'Predicted': y_pred
})

# Add the input features to the DataFrame
# Convert categorical features to numerical using .astype(int) before joining
numerical_X_test = X_test.select_dtypes(include=['number'])  # Selects only numerical columns
predictions_df = predictions_df.join(numerical_X_test, how='left')  # Join with only numerical features

# print(predictions_df.head()) # Display the first few rows

# Add a column indicating whether the prediction was correct
predictions_df['Correct'] = predictions_df['Actual'] == predictions_df['Predicted']

# Group by correctness and calculate summary statistics **only for numeric columns**
misclassification_summary = predictions_df.groupby('Correct').agg({col: 'mean' for col in predictions_df.select_dtypes(include=['number']).columns})
print("\nSummary Statistics by Classification Correctness:\n", misclassification_summary)

# Example: Analyze False Negatives
false_negatives = predictions_df[(predictions_df['Actual'] == 1) & (predictions_df['Predicted'] == 0)]
print("\nFalse Negative Examples:\n", false_negatives)
